name: Vera Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at an organic and health-food wholesaler. We supply independent shops and a few cafés, so I buy oats, nuts, dried fruit, plant milks, from small farms and co-ops as well as bigger brands. A normal day is forecasting what the shops will need in six weeks, chasing small suppliers who don't always answer emails, and checking certificates so we don't sell something labelled organic that isn't.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I've got a chatbot that drafts my supplier emails in three languages, and I built a little forecasting sheet where the AI flags which lines are running hot. It saves me maybe an hour a day. My manager thinks I'm a wizard, which is funny because I mostly just asked good questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, that's sort of a disappointment for me. I was hoping for more. But fine, I'd keep my little tricks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, but the useful bits are worth keeping. Online I'd probably share my forecasting setup so other small wholesalers can use it for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be in a good spot. I'm already ahead on the tools, so I'd be the person in the office others ask for help. The worry is more that Ines, my partner, is a freelance designer, and her clients already pay less than they used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and probably ask for a pay rise based on the time I save. I'd keep saving, we've got about four months put away. And I'd volunteer to train the other buyers on the tools, so they don't feel left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat even. Like a party that ended early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ines's clients pay less. How much does that weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's there in the background. Ines's design income goes up and down, so my salary is the steady one. A plateau doesn't change that, but it doesn't make it worse either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really get a pay rise for saving time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. Bosses tend to take the hour and give you more work. But I'd ask, and I'd bring numbers, because they're my numbers.

say: AI was **overhyped**, but the useful bits are worth keeping.
I'd **share my forecasting** setup free with other small wholesalers.
think: I'm **ahead on the tools**, so I'd be in a good spot.
The real worry is Ines's **freelance income** shrinking.
do: Ask for a **pay rise** backed by the time I save.
Keep **saving** on top of about four months put away.
Volunteer to **train the other buyers** on the tools.
feel: Mild **disappointment**, like a party that ended early.
S0.quote: Bosses tend to take the hour and give you more work.
fieldNote: Vera is **disappointed** by the plateau, unusual among buyers.
Her household's soft spot is **Ines's freelance work**, not her own job.
She'd use her edge to **teach others**, in line with her progressive views.

steps.text: Ask for a pay rise using numbers on time saved
Run a lunchtime session teaching the other buyers the tools
Keep adding to the four months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I recognise. It's basically what I'm already doing, just everywhere and faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if workers get a share of it. I'd post about how companies should cut hours, not people, when AI makes everyone faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well at first. I'd become the person who sets up the buying software and checks its work. But I'm not naive: if one of me can do the work of three, two people go, and those two are my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the rollout of any new buying tools, and I'd push for it to come with a no-layoffs deal. I'd do a short course on data and automation, so I'm not just self-taught. And I'd start freelancing on the side, helping small shops set up their ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited for me, uncomfortable for everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a tension between leading the rollout and protecting your friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Totally. I'd be building the thing that makes their jobs smaller. The only way I can live with that is if I'm loud about how it's used, so I'd put my name to the no-layoffs request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines's work is hit harder than mine in this picture. Design clients already use AI for logos. I'd tell Ines to move into brand strategy, where people pay for taste and a conversation.

say: This is good if **workers get a share**.
Companies should **cut hours, not people** when AI speeds things up.
think: I'd do well at first as the person who **sets up the software**.
If one of me does three jobs, **two friends** lose theirs.
do: Ask to **lead the rollout** with a no-layoffs deal attached.
Take a short course in **data and automation**.
Start **freelancing** to set up ordering for small shops.
feel: **Uncomfortable** about what it means for colleagues.
S1.quote: If one of me can do the work of three, two people go, and those two are my friends.
fieldNote: Vera expects to **gain** personally, but the guilt is real and stated.
She resolves the tension by tying her role to a **no-layoffs** demand.
Ines's design work is the household's **more exposed** income in this picture.

steps.text: Ask to lead the buying software rollout
Take a short online course in data and automation
Start freelancing to set up ordering for small shops
Put her name to a no-layoffs request to management

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one's different. Being good with the tools doesn't help if the tools don't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say this is the moment for a universal basic income and public ownership of some of this tech. I'd be at the marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2028 and probably Ines's too. Both of us are pure screen work. My only edge is that I know the farms and co-ops personally, and that's hands-on in a way, visiting and checking. That gives me maybe three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first months moving toward supplier audits, the farm visits and certificate checks that need someone on site. I'd cut back hard, no trips, and try to get to six months saved. And I'd join a group campaigning for basic income straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My confidence was built on being early, and that doesn't count for much here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our holiday to Portugal next summer, and the second-hand car we were going to buy. We'd stay in the flat because it's cheap for the area. Anything that ties us down goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If the farm audit work takes off, I'd move closer to the farms. Ines can design from anywhere for as long as there's design work left.

say: This is the moment for **basic income** and public ownership of the tech.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, and probably Ines's too.
Knowing the **farms personally** buys me maybe three more years.
do: Move toward **supplier audits** and farm visits within months.
Cut back hard to reach **six months saved**.
feel: Shaken, because my **confidence** came from being early.
S2.quote: Being good with the tools doesn't help if the tools don't need me.
fieldNote: Vera's **tool advantage** collapses under fast AGI, and she says so plainly.
Both household incomes are **screen-based**, which is why she's alarmed.
Farm audits are her **hands-on bridge** through the robot delay.

steps.text: Apply to do supplier audits and farm visits for the wholesaler
Cancel the Portugal trip and the car purchase
Join a campaign group pushing for basic income
Look at moving closer to the farms if audits take off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, that's enough to build something. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: we know it's coming, so let's write the rules now. Shared ownership, retraining money, shorter weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use those five years to squeeze every bit out of being early. Then I'd want to be in work that mixes thinking with being physically somewhere, like farm audits or running a small food co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and use AI to do it in half the time, then use the other half to build a side business auditing small organic farms. I'd get a proper certification as an organic inspector within two years. And I'd put a bit into a co-op shop project with friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but energised. It's a race, but I can see the track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your employer let you do side work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As long as it doesn't compete, I think so. Auditing farms actually helps them, because it keeps supply honest. I'd frame it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a co-op shop a safe bet in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing's safe. But people will still want to buy food from people they know, at least for a while. And a co-op means the gains stay with us.

say: We know AGI is coming, so let's **write the rules now**.
We need **shared ownership**, retraining money and shorter weeks.
think: I'd use five years to squeeze every bit out of **being early**.
Then I'd want **mixed work**, part thinking and part on site.
do: Use AI to halve my workload and build a **farm audit** side business.
Get certified as an **organic inspector** within two years.
Put money into a **co-op shop** with friends.
feel: Like a **race** where I can see the track.
S3.quote: People will still want to buy food from people they know, at least for a while.
fieldNote: With five years, Vera's **adaptability** pays off again.
Her plan blends **side income** and a co-op, matching her values.
She expects her buying job to end but feels **in control** of the landing.

steps.text: Use AI to halve the buying workload
Get certified as an organic inspector within two years
Start auditing small organic farms on the side
Put savings into a co-op shop with friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That feels like a career's worth of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the version where we can plan a fair transition, and that's what I'd campaign for: public retraining money and shorter weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. I'd have time to build the inspection work, maybe a co-op, and still have savings. The robots come for farm work around 2039, and by then I'd be ready to change again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying, keep being the tools person, and save steadily. I'd do the organic inspector certificate in year two or three. And I'd join a local food co-op board to learn how they run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Curious more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make this one go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If companies don't wait for 2036 and start cutting early anyway. That's what I'd watch. If I saw the buying team shrinking in year three, I'd speed everything up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you spend the first year differently from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, much the same, but with an end date in my head. I'd stop drifting. I'd sign up for the inspector course and pay the deposit, so I can't back out.

say: This is the version where we can plan a **fair transition**.
I'd **campaign** for public retraining money and shorter weeks to pay for it.
think: I'd be **fine**, with time to build inspection work.
When robots reach farm work around **2039**, I'd be ready to change again.
do: Keep buying as the **tools person** and save steadily.
Do the **organic inspector** certificate in year two or three.
S4.quote: If I saw the buying team shrinking in year three, I'd speed everything up.
fieldNote: Vera stays **calm** with a decade, trusting her adaptability.
She watches for **early cuts** as the real risk.
Her values steer her toward **co-operative** food work.

steps.text: Keep buying as the team's AI tools person
Pay the deposit for the organic inspector course
Join the board of a local food co-op

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both Ines and I lose our work at the same time and there's no time to build anything. What would help is a basic income, even a small one, and public money for retraining into hands-on food work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about what people would build, not just what they'd lose. I'd like to think some of us would start co-ops and small things that matter.

headlineQuote: My manager thinks I'm a wizard, which is funny because I mostly just asked good questions.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old buyer** at an organic food wholesaler, living with Ines, a freelance designer.
She uses **AI every day** and is the go-to person for tools at work.
She's **progressive**, and wants AI gains shared through shorter hours and co-ops.
She's calm in slow pictures but **alarmed** by AGI in two years, when both incomes go.
Her landing plan is **farm audits** and a food co-op.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her and Ines's screen jobs go at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income**, even a small one.
Public money for **retraining** into hands-on food work.
